title: Men like trees (Mark 8:22–26)
hookLine: the only two-stage healing: first blurry, then clear

cards: If you've ever worn glasses, you know the moment at the eye doctor. They click through the lenses. Better like this?
Or like this? The chart goes from smudge, to almost, to sharp. Today's healing happens a lot like that.
At Bethsaida, people bring a blind man to Jesus, and Mark tells it in two stages, with a pause in the middle. He even tells us what the man saw halfway through.

teach.h: LED BY THE HAND OUT OF TOWN.
teach.b: Jesus takes the man by the hand and leads him out of the village. Picture that walk: a blind man holding a stranger's hand down a dirt road.
Then Jesus spits on his eyes, lays his hands on him, and asks, do you see anything?

teach.h: I SEE MEN AS TREES, WALKING.
teach.b: In the old King James Bible, the man looks up and says, "I see men as trees, walking." Blurry shapes, tall and moving. He can tell they're people only because trees don't walk.
It's an honest answer; he doesn't pretend.
So Jesus lays his hands on his eyes a second time, "and he was restored, and saw every man clearly." Clearly, and far: lexicons give Mark's Greek word as plainly, even at a distance.
Why would Mark tell a healing in two stages? He doesn't say. But look where he puts it.
Just before, Jesus asked the disciples, having eyes, see ye not? Tomorrow, Peter will say who Jesus is, and then, in the very next breath, prove he only half understands it.
Some readers think this blind man is a picture of the disciples. They see something. It's blurry.
People look like trees. They'll need a second touch. Read that way, the story makes room for an honest halfway: the right answer to do you see? can be, sort of.
And in Mark, sort of isn't where it ends. There's a second touch.

how: Some Christians describe faith as a journey rather than a single moment, and some churches pray for healing more than once, taking comfort from the second touch in this story.

he was led out of it by the hand

s: the man's sight came back all at once
first he saw men as trees, walking; after a second touch, he saw every man clearly.
the man said he saw men as trees, walking
blurry, tall shapes that moved: an honest halfway answer.
Jesus healed the man in the middle of the village
he took him by the hand and led him out of the town.

games.q: Jesus has touched your eyes and asks, do you see anything? everything is blurry: people look like walking trees. what do you say?
o: I see men as trees, walking.
games.why: he tells the truth: I see men as trees, walking. Jesus touches him again, and he sees every man clearly.

practice: Think of something in you that's changing slowly: a habit you're breaking, a grief that's easing, a faith or a doubt taking shape.
Ask it honestly, the way Jesus asked the man, do you see anything yet? and if the answer is sort of, blurry, men like trees, let that be all right.
If you pray, you can ask for the second touch; if not, just thank yourself for getting halfway.

wordCard.voice: Clearly, the word for what the blind man finally saw, after a first touch left him seeing only men like trees, walking.

orig.note: Greek: clearly, plainly, even at a distance. Mark 8:25.
